entries.title: Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border
entries.summary: A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said.
entries.content:
Bulgaria

Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border

August 8, 2026

A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said that a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace from the north and exploded near the Romanian border on Saturday morning.

According to the prime minister, there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, as the drone exploded in a sunflower field 100 meters from the border with Romania. He noted that neither of the two neighboring countries had detected the drone.

Radev added that the incident occurred about 1,000 meters from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine.

"We will continue to monitor the situation and strengthen surveillance. Following this incident, we will also redeploy border police anti-drone detection and countermeasure capabilities from the border with Turkey to the border with Romania," Radev said.

What do we know about the drone?

Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his cabinet's security council, Radev did not specify where the drone came from or what type it was.

However, he said that it was believed that the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives given the strength of the blast and the black smoke it produced.

When asked if the drone was civilian or military, Radev said that there was photographic evidence available. However, because the drone was damaged in the explosion, it was impossible to determine its type.

"This is not a toy drone; it's a larger drone," he told journalists, according to the BTA news agency.

However, Radev also mentioned that the drone was not detected in Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size.

Drone incidents on rise in EU countries

In recent months, there have been an increasing number of incidents involving drones in Eastern European countries that are both EU and NATO members and that support Ukraine in its four-and-a-half-year war against Russia's invasion.

The origin of the drone that exploded in Bulgaria and its potential connection to Russia or Ukraine are still unclear. Radev said that teams from the Bulgarian border police and the Ministry of Defense are working to determine the origin of the drone.

Bulgaria's Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said the incident would be raised at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council early next week.

Romania, which borders Ukraine, has faced frequent drone incursions, including crashes on its territory, such as a May incident in which a drone struck an apartment building.

Earlier this week in Germany, an explosive-laden drone was defused at Leipzig Airport, in what Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called a "new level of danger."

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: EU holds talks with big tech over Ceuta misinformation
entries.summary: EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen has called for closer monitoring of social media platforms moving forward, amid the spread of misinformation during the recent migrant influx at Spain's Ceuta.
entries.content:
August 8, 2026

EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen has called for closer monitoring of social media platforms moving forward, amid the spread of misinformation during the recent migrant influx at Spain's Ceuta.

EU Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen has called on social media giants to exercise closer monitoring of their platforms for misinformation, especially "during crisis situations."

Virkkunen was referring to last week's Ceuta border crisis, which European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities say was exacerbated by the spread of misinformation on social media, including TikTok, Telegram and Meta platforms.

Commissioner Virkkunen addressed the disinformation on social media, calling for greater EU monitoring of platforms during crisis situations.

"Platforms must act decisively in keeping the integrity of the digital space, in particular during crisis situations," she wrote on X.

"Monitoring must increase, cooperation with fact-checkers to be strengthened," Virkkunen wrote after a Friday meeting with representatives from TikTok and Meta — which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Social media increasingly central to 'political debate'

A number of the estimated 72,000 people who stormed Ceuta from Morocco said they were attracted by false promises disseminated on social media and that they were lied to about the situation.

Spain and Morocco have also exchanged blame, with authorities in Rabat blaming a Spanish Supreme Court ruling that it says was exploited by human traffickers and misrepresented on social media.

Madrid says Morocco should have done a better job at stopping the tens of thousands of migrants who crossed the border.

In the end, Spanish authorities say 80 people were killed during the course of events.

Moroccan authorities reported that 11 people died on their side of the border.

Rights groups estimate the total number of dead at more than 140.

The situation in Ceuta and the circumstances surrounding it have added more fuel to Europe's ongoing political fight over issues related to immigration and security.

Did misinformation on social media cause the Ceuta crisis?

In Ceuta, migrants pointed to social media messages and videos announcing that the EU border at Ceuta was suddenly open.

Other posts informed people looking to get to the EU that accommodations would be available once they got to the Spanish territory and that they would be bused to the Spanish mainland from there.

Last week, EU member states convened an emergency meeting at which representatives mulled early-warning systems and social media monitoring as potential levers for improving the bloc's shared assessment capabilities in emerging situations.

Virkkunen said the EU would continue that discussion on Monday.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: When German Catholics and Protestants share a church
entries.summary: Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed in Germany. But there is a new, unique development.
entries.content:
Germany

When German Catholics and Protestants share a church

August 8, 2026

Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed in Germany. But there is a new, unique development.

From the outside, the Catholic church in Mannheim's Neuostheim district appears to be a typical 1950s church building: a relatively simple structure, nothing particularly remarkable about it. Yet St. Pius is truly unique. In this place of worship, Catholic and Protestant Christians celebrate services sharing the same space and taking turns in gathering around the same altar for Communion and the Eucharist.

"It actually began in the early 1970s," Annette Hübner, a Catholic parishioner, told DW. The 57-year-old has lived in the district with her family for more than half a century and is a member of the parish team. At the time, the parish priest of St. Pius was committed to fostering cooperation with the Protestant community and began holding ecumenical services in 1970. Then, at the end of 2009, the nearby Protestant St. Thomas Church sustained extensive water damage, and the building was found to be beyond repair.

What began as a temporary arrangement gradually evolved into a lasting solution. That lasting solution, in turn, grew into a genuine ecumenical friendship.

"It became increasingly clear that it made sense to continue working together," Hübner recalled. A banner on the facade of St. Pius proclaims: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." What may sound like a theological phrase from a Sunday sermon is part of everyday life here, on weekdays as much as on Sundays.

Catholics and Protestants under one roof: Germany is home to 65 so-called Simultankirchen (shared churches). Their joint use was mandated by secular rulers soon after the Reformation and the resulting division of the Church. In some cases, detailed regulations even specified who was allowed to enter the church and at what times. The best-known examples are Altenberg Cathedral near Cologne and St. Peter's Protestant Cathedral in the eastern German city of Bautzen in Saxony.

In hospital and airport chapels, shared use by different Christian denominations is now almost taken for granted. A similar trend, however, is increasingly emerging in ordinary parish communities. Protestant and Catholic churches in Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia had already begun addressing the issue in 2017, during the commemorations marking the 500th anniversary of Martin Luther's Reformation.

"What If We All Moved In Together?" is the title of the Practical Guide to the Ecumenical Use of Churches and Parish Halls. The publication presents examples from the dioceses of Cologne and Aachen, as well as Essen, Münster and Paderborn.

The guide repeatedly points to the "accelerating reduction in church buildings." According to official church statistics for 2025, Germany had 24,500 Catholic and 21,100 Protestant churches, ranging from small chapels to grand cathedrals. Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed.

Attending a Protestant church was once considered 'a sin'

Examples of new shared church spaces can be found in both western and eastern Germany. In Schildow, on the northern outskirts of Berlin, only one church is expected to remain in use in the future: the larger and more prominent Protestant church. The Archdiocese of Berlin's press office  describes the initiative as "an ecumenical project with exemplary character." Its statement also hints at the significance of this development: "For all the ecumenical openness that is now taken for granted," the Catholic participants still remember "earlier times when even attending a Protestant church was considered a sin."

Small congregations in the East

Catholic bishops in eastern Germany are quite accustomed to celebrating Mass in Protestant churches. For major occasions such as confirmations or parish anniversaries, the generally smaller Catholic churches are often unable to accommodate everyone. In such cases, their Protestant counterparts are often happy to provide the necessary space.

The German Bishops' Conference is also currently addressing the issue and plans to publish a practical guide on the subject. Here, too, the focus is on declining membership, church buildings that are no longer needed, financial constraints, and the potential for shared use.

Two altars merged into one

But St. Pius in Mannheim is different. It is far more than a temporary arrangement born of necessity. Here, the two congregations have developed a deep and wide-ranging form of cooperation. Between 2020 and 2022, the church underwent extensive renovation and redesign. The place where the altar once stood is now occupied by the baptismal font, serving as a shared focal point for both churches. A new altar, crafted from red and grey stone, now stands in the nave.

"The red sandstone comes from the altar of the Protestant church, and the grey travertine from the altar of the Catholic church," Hübner explained. Both were crushed and cast together to form the new altar. Parts of its surface are completely smooth, while others remain rough, with visible grooves and fissures. "It was a beautiful symbol of the relationship between Protestants and Catholics. We want to come together. But there are still points of friction and unresolved questions."

Careful legal arrangements

St. Birgitta-Thomas Church in the northern German city of Kiel can likewise look back on decades of ecumenical cooperation. Since 1980, the Catholic parish of St. Birgitta and the Protestant Thomas congregation have shared both the church and the parish hall. Here, too, this "sharing" is governed by carefully defined legal arrangements.

Officially, the church belongs to the Catholic parish, while the parish hall belongs to the Protestant congregation. "But we use both parts of the complex jointly and on an equal footing," Pastor Rebekka Ulrich told DW. With a smile, she adds: "The Protestant side leased the printer, but the Catholic side uses it too."

The 36-year-old pastor sees "an incredible number of points of overlap." These include joint worship services, celebrations and ecumenical dialogue. Each year, the two denominations adopt a shared motto. A hymn of the month, selected alternately from the Protestant hymnal and the Catholic Gotteslob, is sung by the entire congregation during services.

A shortage of clergymen and organists

The close partnership extends even to church music: both congregations share the same organist. "On Sundays, he accompanies the Catholic Mass at 9:30 a.m. and then the Protestant service at 11:00 a.m." If only everything were that simple. As Ulrich explains, the steadily declining number of Catholic priests is creating growing challenges for the Catholic side.

In Mannheim, Annette Hübner described the process as a journey that was long but, in her view, well worth the effort. The number of clergy is declining in both the Catholic and Protestant churches. At the local level, services of the Word conducted without a priest or pastor are becoming increasingly common.

Even the Eastern Christian tradition has found a place here. Since 1971, Mannheim has been home to the "Eastern Church Center Cyril and Methodius," which has been based at St. Pius from the very beginning. Once a month, a Catholic liturgy is celebrated according to the Byzantine Rite. Since the renovation, the church entrance area has included a specially designed space with icons and a symbolic iconostasis. All of this exists under a single church roof.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Germany news: Trucking rules eased as rivers run low
entries.summary: Several states will let trucks use motorways on Sundays and holidays as freight shipping is hampered by low water levels. The body of a German sailor missing for days has been found in the southern Aegean. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Trucking rules eased as rivers run low

Published August 8, 2026last updated August 8, 2026

Several states will let trucks use motorways on Sundays and holidays as freight shipping is hampered by low water levels. The body of a German sailor missing for days has been found in the southern Aegean. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's main industrial association welcomes the easing of restrictions on truck traffic as river water levels become too low for cargo vessels
  • A German sailor missing for days in the southern Aegean has been found dead, according to Greek media
  • The far-right AfD is kicking off its election campaign in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

Here is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany that are hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 8-9, 2026:

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section European team ends 100-day 'Mars' sojourn in Cologne

European team ends 100-day 'Mars' sojourn in Cologne

Six men and women from six different countries on Friday ended their 100-day stay in cramped, artificially lit isolation as part of a study to prepare future space missions to the moon, Mars and beyond.

The participants, from Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and Portugal, are now able to return to their daily lives — following a recovery phase — after leaving the simulation facility at the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) in the western city of Cologne.

The goal of the SOLIS100 study was conducted on behalf of the European Space Agency (ESA) and aimed to investigate the effects of long-duration space missions  on health and performance.

The participants had to live from non-perishable foodstuffs and were not allowed personal contact with family or friends.

 

 Every day, they carried out scientific work, medical data collection, a strict exercise program and station maintenance.  

Skip next section Culture Minister Weimer calls for Infantino's resignation

Culture Minister Weimer calls for Infantino's resignation

Wolfram Weimer, the commissioner for culture and media, has become the first member of the federal government to call for FIFA President Gianni Infantino to step down.

"Infantino has seriously damaged world football with his planned sell-off of the World Cup," he told the German DPA news agency on Saturday.

"He has lost the trust of the European football community and should not stand for re-election next year," he said.

Weimer called on the German Football Federation (DFB) to show "active resistance" against Infantino.

"With its 24,000 clubs and eight million members, the DFB is the largest sports federation in the world (by individual registered members). Its voice carries weight," he said.

Infantino has faced a storm of criticism since he unveiled plans last week to sell World Cup rights to private investors for billions.

He withdrew the proposal after major protests, including a threat by UEFA to boycott the World Cup.

Skip next section Two drones spotted above military base after Leipzig Airport incident

Two drones spotted above military base after Leipzig Airport incident

Two drones were sighted flying late on Thursday above a military base in Mechernich in western Germany, near the Belgian border, authorities said on Saturday.

A German armed forces spokesperson said the drones were sighted at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, which media say hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems.

Among other things, US Patriot systems play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks.

The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after a drone carrying explosives was found near a runway at Leipzig/Halle Airport, with media saying it was discovered near several Ukrainian cargo planes.

A number of sightings of drones at sensitive sites in Germany in recent times has raised concerns about the penetration of NATO airspace by the unmanned aircraft and the possibility of hostile foreign involvement.

German government officials have not blamed any foreign countries publicly ​for the Leipzig incident, ⁠but some lawmakers have accused Russia of being behind it.

The Russian Embassy in Berlin on Friday dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation" and said Russia was once more being accused of hostile actions without evidence.

Skip next section Far-right AfD set to kick off election campaign in eastern state

Far-right AfD set to kick off election campaign in eastern state

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is to hold an event in the afternoon as it starts its election campaign in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The event will be led by the party's candidate to become state premier, Leif-Erik Holm, its top candidate Enrico Schult and its general secretary, Dario Seifert.

The AfD chairman from the state of Saxony, Jörg Urban, will be a guest at the event in the city of Stralsund.

The anti-immigration party is currently polling at around 36% in pre-election surveys in the state, making it the strongest force.

Several other state chapters of the party have been designated as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, but they do not include the one in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Skip next section Missing German sailor found in southern Aegean

Missing German sailor found in southern Aegean

A German man who had gone missing for days while sailing in the south Aegean has been found dead in waters west of the island of Symi, Greek media have reported, citing the coastguard.

He was among a group of eight people from Germany whose boat was swept away by the current off the island while they were swimming near the vessel on Sunday evening, according to the Greek news agency ANA-MPA.

Two of the eight managed to swim ashore and five were rescued, but the man whose body has now been found remained unaccounted for until now.

Skip next section Industrial association calls for quick easing of motorway restrictions for trucks

Industrial association calls for quick easing of motorway restrictions for trucks

Germany's main industry association, the Federation of German Industries (BDI), has welcomed plans to allow trucks to transport goods on motorways throughout the week as cargo ships are hampered by low river water levels.

"The federal government is demonstrating its ability to act in this extreme situation," Holger Lösch, BDI deputy managing director told the Rheinische Post newspaper on Saturday. "The agreed measures must now be implemented quickly."

Lösch said moving goods to road and rail could ease the disruption and stabilize supply chains but conceded that it would not fully offset lost shipping capacity.

In Germany, most trucks are banned from using the motorways, or Autobahnen, on Sundays and public holidays, with exceptions made for vehicles transporting, for example, perishable foodstuffs.

Several German states have temporarily relaxed the restrictions to allow more freight to be shifted from waterways to roads.

Environmental groups have criticized the easing off of restrictions, saying the low river levels have been partly driven by global warming and that the underlying problem would not be solved by higher truck traffic.

The Federal Association for Road Haulage and Logistics (BGL) has warned that driving and rest time regulations would still have to be adhered to despite the additional days.

Spokesman Dirk Engelhardt told the Rheinische Post on Thursday that there would thus be no increase in available driving time.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the increasingly depleted Rhine!

The  lack of water in the Rhine and other rivers is hampering cargo shipping and has prompted the government to propose easing rules restricting the use of motorways by trucks on Sunday and public holidays.

Though welcomed by industrial associations, environmentalists and truck driver representatives are not so sure about the idea.

Meanwhile, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD)is to hold an event in Stralsund to kick off its election campaign in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania ahead of a vote scheduled for September 20. 

Read on here for more on these and other stories from Europe's biggest economy.

entries.title: India wary of potential 100% US tariffs over Russian oil
entries.summary: The US Senate passed a sanctions bill that could result in tariffs on India as a major consumer of Russian oil. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
India

India wary of potential 100% US tariffs over Russian oil

Published August 8, 2026last updated August 8, 2026

The US Senate passed a sanctions bill that could result in tariffs on India as a major consumer of Russian oil. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian exports to the US could face 100% levy
  • The tariff threat comes after the US Senate passed its latest Russia sanctions bill
  • India officially maps 27 places in Arunachal Pradesh state

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Saturday, August 8: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Jharkhand: Deadlock continues despite state government talks with protesters

Jharkhand: Deadlock continues despite state government talks with protesters

The Jharkhand government on Saturday held a second round of talks with various factions of the students protesting in Jharkhand over exam irregularities. 

While the students said that the government heard their demands, they have decided to continue the protest until the issues are taken up with Chief Minister Hemant Soren before deciding whether to end their hunger strike.

The state government has held meetings with two different delegations of student protesters. Students from both factions have said they are prepared to march towards the Assembly on Monday.

The students are demanding the scrapping of the 14th Civil Services Preliminary Examination conducted by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) on July 2.

They are also seeking investigations by the Central Bureau of Investigation and the Enforcement Directorate into alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations conducted by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission.

Skip next section Heavy rainfall wreaks havoc in Delhi

Heavy rainfall wreaks havoc in Delhi

On Friday, Delhi recorded record rainfall, India Meteorological Department (IMD) records show, making it the wettest first week of August in over a decade.

As the heavy rain lashed the city, several highways and streets were submerged under up to four feet of water, disrupting daily life.

The IMD issued a red alert for the city.

The waterlogged roads brought traffic to a standstill, especially in the adjoining Gurugram.

According to the IMD, the showers were triggered by multiple low-pressure systems passing through Delhi, southwest Uttar Pradesh and neighboring regions.

Skip next section India officially names 27 places in disputed Arunachal Pradesh to counter China

India officially names 27 places in disputed Arunachal Pradesh to counter China

India has formally assigned names for 27 sites in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the state which Chinaalso claims.

An official statement from the Home Ministry said the Indian government, in consultation with the government of Arunachal Pradesh, "identified a total of 27 places or features in Arunachal Pradesh, by standard place and feature names on the official maps of Survey of India (SoI)."

"Identifying them formally on the Survey of India map of Arunachal Pradesh is aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large," the statement said.

The sites include mountain passes, high-altitude lakes, villages and a monument.

"There has been a lot of ambiguity regarding the maps. China uses this to give fictitious names to Arunachal Pradesh’s territories, which are part of sovereign India," an anonymous official told Indian newspaper Hindustan Times.

The two nations have accused each other of trying to seize territory along their de facto border, known as the Line of Actual Control (LAC), which India claims is 3,488 kilometers (2,167 miles) long and China says is shorter.

The move comes after India and China held talks to discuss the border situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).

Skip next section US passes bill threatening 100% tariffs on India

US passes bill threatening 100% tariffs on India

The US Senate has passed a bill that would allow the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries that purchase Russian oil and gas, including India and China.

The bill, according to US lawmakers, is aimed at curtailing Russia's funding for its war in Ukraine.

The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was passed with an overwhelming vote of 86-11.

Why is the bill troublesome for India?

India is among the world's top importers of Russian oil and gas, and its purchase of discounted Russian crudes has gone up since the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022.

With the conflict in the Middle East disrupting energy markets, Russian crude has become an important alternative source for Indian refiners.

If 100% tariffs are imposed on Indian goods exported to the US, it will make them significantly more expensive, which could force US importers to look for alternative suppliers.

The bill does not automatically impose tariffs, but rather allows US President Donald Trump the discretion to impose them, with the implementation depending on the final law and subsequent executive decisions.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from the DW New Delhi bureau bringing you all the latest updates from across India.

After a full day of heavy downpour in Delhi and the adjoining areas, the capital has a brief respite from the rain. However, weather agencies have forecast more rain in the next few days.

Delhi is apprehensive after the US Senate passed a bill that could impose tariffs of up to 100% on India, China and three other countries heavily reliant on Russian oil and gas.

Meanwhile, a day after India and China held talks on border security in Arunachal Pradesh, New Delhi formally named 27 places in the northeastern state to counter China's attempts to create "baseless narratives."

Stay tuned for all this and more.

entries.title: Typhoon Dolphin hits Japan as China braces for coming storm
entries.summary: A typhoon is lashing Japan's south, causing injuries and blackouts. It is now headed for China, where ports have been closed in preparation.
entries.content:
Japan

Typhoon Dolphin hits Japan as China braces for coming storm

August 8, 2026

A typhoon is lashing Japan's south, causing injuries and blackouts. It is now headed for China, where ports have been closed in preparation.

Typhoon Dolphin raged over Japan's southern regions on Saturday, causing some injuries and blackouts.

Okinawa and Amami island in Kagoshima prefecture were the areas expected to be worst affected.

The storm is expected to move on to China, making landfall along its eastern and southern ‌coast between late Sunday and early Monday, with Chinese authorities shutting down ports and ferry services ahead of the storm.

What do we know about Typhoon Dolphin in Japan?

  • The typhoon has brought maximum sustained winds of 162 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour) and ​gusts reaching ‌216 kph
  • Authorities in Okinawa prefecture said 240 people had taken shelter at evacuation centers in the region on Friday
  • Five elderly people were reported to have suffered non-life-threatening injuries
  • Japan Meteorological Agency forecast strong winds, heavy rain and high waves in the Okinawa region through Sunday
  • The Naha Airport on Okinawa Island said it closed on Friday, and all domestic and international flights in and out of Naha, the prefectural capital, have been canceled
  • Power was cut to some 14,000 buildings in Okinawa

What preparations is China making for Typhoon Dolphin?

The China National Meteorological Centre Typhoon Dolphin has said Typhoon Dolphin will probably make landfall between the city of Zhoushan in Zhejiang province and the city of Fuding in Fujian province.

Zhejiang has raised its coastal typhoon alert to its highest level, while ceasing port operations and suspending 162 passenger ferry routes.

The storm is expected to bring rain and strong winds to eastern China, including parts of Shanghai, through August 12.

Some parts of eastern Zhejiang could be in for a deluge, forecasters say, with more than 600 mm (23.6 inches) of rain possible.

Ningbo ⁠Lishe ​International Airport in Zhejiang said it will stop its operations from 11:30 ​p.m. (1530 GMT) on Saturday and suspend all flights on Sunday.

Taiwan-China tensions over typhoon restrictions

Taiwan, where 63 international flights have been cancelled, is also expected to experience heavy rain in the north over the weekend.

New political friction between Taiwan and China has also arisen after Beijing ordered that ships passing through ⁠the Taiwan Strait must heed ​its traffic control instructions amid the typhoon.

Taipei has slammed Beijing's injunctions as "ridiculous," saying that Beijing has no right to restrict access to international waters.

"The unreasonable and crude statement ‌by ​the relevant Chinese Communist departments reflects an ignorance, disregard, and trampling of international order and norms. It is utterly ridiculous!" Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said in a statement late ​on Friday.

China regards the democratically governed island as a breakaway territory of its own and also claims to own the strategic strait, a stance rejected by both Taipei and Washington.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Germany debates reintroducing mandatory civilian service
entries.summary: Social organizations are skeptical about the government's ideas for a civilian service program that youths could choose as an alternative should Germany reinstate mandatory military conscription.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany debates reintroducing mandatory civilian service

August 8, 2026

Social organizations are skeptical about the government's ideas for a civilian service program that youths could choose as an alternative should Germany reinstate mandatory military conscription.

Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, guarantees that no person can be forced into armed military service. Should the government reinstate mandatory conscription, a civilian-service alternative would have to be established for people who invoke their right to refuse military service on moral grounds as conscientious objectors.

Germany's federal government is making arrangements for this. The Family Affairs Ministry, led by Karin Prien, of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), has confirmed that in recent months it reached out to 23 large associations and organizations to ask what capacities they had to offer if civilian service were reinstated. Of those, 22 indicated a general willingness to offer opportunities for civilian service participants.

Thorsten Frei, the parliamentary group leader of the center-right bloc of the CDU and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) in the Bundestag, told the German broadcasters RTL and ntv that it was "very clever and correct" for the Family Affairs Ministry to prepare in this way. However, Frei said, there are no new developments in the discussion surrounding the possible reinstatement of conscription.

Bundeswehr seeks soldiers

After lengthy negotiations, the coalition government of the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) agreed that military service would remain voluntary in Germany for now. Whether this remains the case will depend on how many soldiers the German armed forces, the Bundeswehr, can recruit in the coming months and years.

The goal is to increase the number of troops from 185,000 to at least 260,000 by 2030 in order to strengthen national defenses and fulfill NATO requirements. Or, as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) put it: The Bundeswehr should become the strongest conventional army in Europe.

The so-called new military service, which has been in force since the start of this year, is also expected to boost the recruitment effort. It combines improved conditions for volunteers with responsibilities applying to all 18-year-old men: They must fill out a questionnaire to answer if they would be prepared to serve in the army.

They are required to undergo medical examinations and to state whether they are interested in joining the armed forces. However, they maintain the constitutional right to refuse military service as conscientious objectors.

Bundeswehr applications increase

Even without reinstating compulsory military service, the recruitment drive is on track to reach its target for 2026, according to a June forecast by Germany's Defense Ministry. However, only about 530 young men have voluntarily signed up to the military as a direct result of the Bundeswehr questionnaire in 2026.

So, though a return to conscription is not currently expected, it remains an option for the government. Combined with civilian service, it was in place in Germany (starting in West Germany in 1956) until 2011, when it was suspended. However, it was not removed from the constitution. So, parliament can reactivate it by law if needed, for example if the country's security situation changes.

The alternative, mandatory civilian service (Zivildienst) usually involved working in a hospital or care home for several months.

This civilian service was replaced in 2011 by the Bundesfreiwilligendienst , or federal volunteer service, which is open to people of all ages and genders. Conscription only applied to men.

'Government-mandated cheap labor'

Major German welfare organizations have pledged their support should civilian service be relaunched. At the same time, they warn against false expectations. The general consensus is that civilian service is no fix for acute staff shortages in the social services sector. Instead of relying on obligation, the federal government should instead strengthen the optional engagement of young people.

"Our main wish is improved conditions for the voluntary services," Eva Maria Welskop-Deffaa, the president of the German Caritas Association, told the public broadcaster ARD. "And there is still a lot of room for improvement on that."

Germany's opposition parties have also criticized a possible return to mandatory civilian service. According to the socialist Left Party, the state "should not dictate how young people spend a year of their lives," co-leader Ines Schwerdtner said. That applied to both military and civilian service. On the other side, young people should not serve as "stopgaps for a welfare state" which the government "has been systematically underfunding for years." Nursing care, emergency services and social institutions did not need "government-mandated cheap labor," Schwerdtner told the Funke media group.

In any case, the Family Affairs Ministry sees a need to revise and modernize the current civilian service law. It plans to present its proposals after Germany's summer recess.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Ceuta: Spain sets up border controls on travelers from Italy
entries.summary: Spain had warned Italy it would impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.
entries.content:
Spain

Ceuta: Spain sets up border controls on travelers from Italy

August 8, 2026

Spain had warned Italy it would impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy. The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain.

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week. 

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

What did Spain say about checks on travelers from Italy?

The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy.

Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population." 

Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years. 

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain?

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

entries.title: Colombia: Trump ally De la Espriella takes office
entries.summary: Conservative Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president, promising to crack down on armed drug gangs.
entries.content:
Colombia

Colombia: Trump ally De la Espriella takes office

August 8, 2026

Conservative Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president, promising to crack down on armed drug gangs.

Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president on Friday, promising to boost ties with the United States and tackle armed groups linked to the drug trade.

The 48-year-old ex-lawyer lurches the Andean nation to the right, taking office after winning a close June 21 runoff against Sen. Ivan Cepeda, an ally of outgoing President Gustavo Petro.

What happened at the inauguration?

In a speech shortly after his swearing-in, De la Espriella vowed once again to wipe out "narcoterrorism" in the South American country.

"The option of dialogue is completely exhausted," he said, referring to his predecessor, who had promoted a peaceful resolution to the crisis.

De la Espriella then promised to restore "order, authority and freedom" to the South American nation.

"There will be no room for maneuvers that undermine the stability of the nation," said the hardline leader, who has spoken of opening mega-prisons to house captured rebels and drug dealers.

Instead of the capital Bogota, the inauguration took place at a university in the southwestern city of Cali.

Colombia’s third-largest city is located near major drug-trafficking corridors and the Pacific coast, and is a regular scene of violence by rival groups.

Among the VIP guests were King Felipe VI of Spain, acting US Attorney General Todd Blanche, FIFA President Gianni Infantino and Latin American presidents, including Argentina's Javier Milei, Ecuador's Daniel Noboa and Chile's Jose Antonio Kast.

Outgoing president Petro declined to attend the ceremony and called for mass protests Friday, claiming election fraud without providing evidence.

Who is Abelardo de la Espriella?

The 48-year-old is a former lawyer and businessman who has never held public office.

He funded his campaign with the profits from his law firm and other business ventures in the agri-food, real estate and fashion sectors.

The self-styled "El Tigre" (The Tiger) plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel to aid his war on rebel groups, including remnants of the FARC guerrillas, who waged an armed conflict that peaked in the 1990s and 2000s.

De la Espriella won the backing of US President Donald Trump after committing Colombia to a US-backed coalition to fight drug trafficking, dubbed the "Shield of the Americas."

He has also offered to launch joint military operations with Washington and even host US troops on Colombian soil.

The millionaire has also announced plans to resume diplomatic relations with Israel and sever them with Cuba and Nicaragua.

De la Espriella's win is another point for right-wing politics in Latin America, after electoral victories from Chile to Costa Rica, having also promised to crack down on security issues.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Iceland’s EU vote: A nation divided over Europe
entries.summary: Security concerns, control over fishing rights and rising living costs are shaping Iceland's debate over whether to restart talks on joining the European Union.
entries.content:
Iceland

Iceland’s EU vote: A nation divided over Europe

August 7, 2026

Security concerns, control over fishing rights and rising living costs are shaping Iceland's debate over whether to restart talks on joining the European Union.

The white church stands alone in the Icelandic countryside. Wind sweeps across the Hvalfjord. Kristjan Ingolfsson, a retired bishop, lives here beside Hallgrimskirkja church in Saubaer, surrounded by silence and vast open landscapes.

But far from this quiet corner of western Iceland, the debate over Europe is heating up. At the end of August, voters will decide whether to reopen accession talks with the European Union.  The referendum is not about joining the EU immediately, but about restarting negotiations that were suspended more than a decade ago.

"[Icelandic] people are a bit different to the mainland folks, who always have to think about borders. We have no border, just the sea all around," Kristjan Ingolfsson says.

"That gives a specific feeling of freedom. And I believe that's also part of the whole discussion, that people want to be free."

Whether campaigning for or against closer ties with Brussels, many Icelanders frame the debate around the same ideas: freedom, independence, and sovereignty.

The 'Yes' campaign

At the headquarters of the pro-European group in the capital, Reykjavik, supporters are celebrating the official launch of the campaign. The small office is packed, with volunteers spilling onto the pavement in the afternoon sun. Young people mingle with pensioners. A DJ provides music while beer and soft drinks are kept chilled in ice buckets.

At the center of it all is Snaeros Sindradottir, executive director of the 'Yes' campaign. The 34-year-old mother normally runs an art gallery, but that work is now on hold. Instead, she spends her days campaigning for a closer relationship with Europe.

The referendum is taking place at a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty.  US President Donald Trump's threats toward neighboring Greenland have become part of Iceland's debate over Europe, says Snaeros Sindradottir. 

"And it's not a very comforting fact that Trump has mispronounced Greenland as Iceland on several occasions."

Iceland, with its population of about 400,000, has no standing army. Protection is provided through NATO, of which Iceland is a founding member. The country also has a bilateral defense agreement with Washington. During the Cold War, the US maintained an important military base near Reykjavik, although its permanent troop presence ended in 2006. 

"I think security would definitely be increased if we enter the EU," says Snaeros Sindradottir.

"Given the situation in the United States, it would be wiser to lean [on] our true allies and friends in Europe."

Iceland is already closely tied to Europe. The country belongs to the European Economic Area (EEA), allowing free movement of goods, services, capital and people between Iceland and most EU countries, even though the island nation is not an EU member. It is also part of the passport-free Schengen zone.

Pawel Bartoszek, chairman of parliament's foreign affairs committee, points to Iceland's small and relatively volatile currency.

"It has cost us much higher inflation and interest rates compared to continental Europe," he says.

Bartoszek argues that joining the euro in the future could lower borrowing costs for households and businesses. Mortgage rates of 8 to 9% are common in Iceland, while borrowers elsewhere in Europe often pay roughly half as much.

The 'No' campaign

In downtown Reykjavik, campaigners from the anti-EU movement are making the opposite case. They have set up a small table where they hand out leaflets and "No" campaign badges. Haraldur Olafsson, a physics professor, currently spends up to 12 hours a day campaigning against membership.

"We are basically here to explain to the people that being members of the European Union is a huge step away from democracy."

"We are giving power to someone else who will make rules that we cannot control," he adds.

For years, Haraldur Olafsson has campaigned against joining the EU. He is the president of the Heimssyn organization, which belongs to the 'No' camp.

The 'No' campaign's stand is quiet today. Tourists crowd the square opposite parliament, every now and then Olafsson is approached by acquaintances. This is Iceland. People know each other here.

"I do not know anybody in Iceland who fears either the Russians or the Americans," Haraldur Olafsson says.

"Really, I don't think these international matters matter a lot when it comes to local politics. The only threat comes from the European Union. The European Union is the only big power in the world that wants to govern Iceland, that wants to set the laws in Iceland and wants to pass judgment."

Supporters of EU membership reject this argument, saying that as an EU member Iceland would participate in decision-making rather than simply follow rules set elsewhere.

Rich fishing industry

Iceland's thriving fishing industry is one of the foundations of the country's prosperity. That is why the debate over possible EU membership has become highly emotional, with both sides arguing over whether the European Union would gain control over Iceland's valuable marine resources.

"The European Union has nothing to say about the natural resources in Iceland — the sea, the fish," Haraldur Olafsson says.

"The European Union doesn't have the final word on energy, which is a very important natural resource for Iceland."

"The economy of Iceland is very different from the economy of Europe. The main disadvantage is that the EU would take over the administration of [our] natural resources," he argues.

Haraldur Olafsson heads down to Reykjavik's harbor. Here he meets former fisherman Agust Österby, who is standing on his wooden boat, fixing an old window frame. Österby first went to sea with his father when he was six years old. Today, he restores wooden boats.

Icelanders, he says, are stubborn and independent by nature.

"It is somehow in our genes to deal with [things] ourselves — to deal with life, the sea and the weather."

He adds: "We will never give our freedom to the European Union. We know exactly how to do things in Iceland. We don't need help from abroad."

The former fisherman says he does not think Icelanders feel threatened by anyone — not even Donald Trump.

Referendum to break the deadlock

The belief that Iceland can simply keep a low profile and avoid international pressure is something political scientist Audunn Arnorsson disagrees with. He fears the strategy "might backfire."

If Iceland were ever to face pressure similar to that experienced by Greenland from its "big brother in the West," having the possibility of EU accession could prove valuable, including access to the bloc's common customs protection. 

Iceland had already begun accession negotiations once before, in 2010, following the banking and economic crisis. They were later suspended after a change in government and never resumed. Audunn Arnorsson argues that holding a referendum became the only way to break the political deadlock over whether Iceland should reopen negotiations.

Debate dividing Iceland

Members of Iceland's parliament are also divided over whether the country should resume accession talks with the European Union. The debate cuts across traditional party lines.

Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, leader of the opposition Independence Party, believes that a small nation like Iceland may have a bigger voice outside the European Union than inside.

"In the European Parliament, we would have approximately six seats out of 726. We are afraid that we will just disappear in this mass that the European Union is."

Smaller EU member states such as Malta, Luxembourg and Cyprus also hold the minimum allocation of six seats in the European Parliament.

For Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, joining the EU is not the solution for strengthening Iceland's security.

"Our strength lies in NATO and our bilateral agreement with the United States of America. And we have not had any discussion from [the] American side that they want to change that agreement that we have had here in Iceland for decades."

But something else concerns the opposition leader deeply: the divisions the debate has created within families and friendships.

"We are building a wound that won't heal [for] years. We can't survive in this harsh country if we don't have solidarity between us, so that we can fight Mother Nature."

Opinion polls predict a tight race, with support for and opposition to closer EU integration running neck and neck. Both camps are now fighting for the same group: the many undecided voters who are likely to determine the result on August 29.

A 'yes' vote would not mean EU membership. It would only open accession talks — with a second referendum required before Iceland could ultimately join the bloc.

But former bishop Kristjan Ingolfsson is confident: "No matter how it turns out — we will remain one people and [it will] not build walls between us."
